title-group.article-title: A self-controlled case series to evaluate the effects of clinical trial eligibility criteria on biologic-associated reductions in severe asthma exacerbations: an analysis of the CHRONICLE study

related-article.article-title: Are lung function measurements necessary to evaluate efficacy of biologics in asthma?

caption.p: Overview of the study. RCT: randomised controlled trial; FENO: fractional exhaled nitric oxide; BEC: blood eosinophil count.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: The trade-offs between regulatory preferences, trial success probability, and patient exclusion by eligibility criteria in randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of biologics for severe asthma remain poorly understood. We assessed biologic effectiveness and effect modification by nine RCT-derived criteria in a large real-world cohort of subspecialist-treated patients with severe asthma.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: CHRONICLE was a multicentre, prospective, noninterventional cohort of adults (aged ≥18 years) in the United States of America with severe asthma (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT03373045). We performed a meta-analysis of six RCTs to estimate pooled rate ratios for United States Food and Drug Administration approved biologics and compared with incidence rate ratios (IRRs) from a self-controlled case-series using CHRONICLE data, analysing severe asthma exacerbation rates during biologic-exposed and unexposed periods. Subgroup analyses examined between-group comparisons (inclusion versus exclusion) across nine RCT-based criteria.

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: Biologics reduced exacerbation rates in both RCT meta-analysis (rate ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.47–0.60) and real-world self-controlled case-series of 480 patients from 85 sites (enrolled between 28 February 2018 and 28 October 2024) (IRR 0.43, 95% CI 0.39–0.48). Significant effect modification (ratio of ratios, ratio of IRR (95% CI), with exclusion as the reference) was observed for smoking history (0.50, 0.38–0.66), exacerbation history (0.49, 0.36–0.65), exhaled nitric oxide fraction (0.63, 0.42–0.92), and blood eosinophil count (0.65, 0.51–0.82). No significant differences were observed for COPD, bronchiectasis, or forced expiratory volume in 1 s based criteria, which excluded the most patients in the cohort.

sec.title: Interpretation
sec.p: Criteria based on elevated type 2 biomarkers, minimal smoking, and exacerbation history enrich trial populations likely to benefit from biologics. Spirometry-based exclusions appear to have limited influence on treatment response, and there is a risk that they unduly restrict generalisability.

p.bold: Spirometry-based exclusions have limited influence on biologic treatment response and unduly restrict generalisability of clinical trials

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Severe asthma accounts for approximately 5–10% of patients with asthma and contributes to ∼50% of healthcare costs of asthma-related diseases annually [1, 2]. For patients with severe asthma, symptoms can remain difficult-to-treat or be uncontrolled. Patients with uncontrolled severe asthma commonly experience exacerbations that require treatment with systemic corticosteroids and can result in significant healthcare utilisation [1].

Several treatment options have been proposed to reduce the incidence of severe asthma exacerbations, including high-dose inhaled corticosteroids with additional controllers, monoclonal antibody agents and maintenance use of systemic corticosteroids [1, 2]. Currently, there are six United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved monoclonal antibody therapies (hereafter “biologics”) indicated for patients with severe uncontrolled asthma in the United States of America (USA) [1, 2]. These include omalizumab (approved in 2003) [3], mepolizumab (approved in 2015) [4], reslizumab (approved in 2016) [5], benralizumab (approved in 2017) [6], dupilumab (approved in 2018) [7] and tezepelumab (approved in 2021) [8]. These biologics for treating severe asthma vary in terms of mechanism and eligibility criteria [9, 10]. Although omalizumab (anti-IgE) is approved for the treatment of moderate-to-severe allergic asthma, three anti-interleukin (IL)5/IL5 receptor (IL5R) biologics (mepolizumab, reslizumab and benralizumab) are approved for treatment of severe eosinophilic asthma, dupilumab (anti-IL4R) is approved to treat moderate-to-severe eosinophilic or oral corticosteroid-dependent asthma, and tezepelumab (anti-thymic stromal lymphopoietin) is approved treat to severe asthma regardless of phenotype (e.g. eosinophilic or allergic) [11–13].

Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) are considered the “gold standard” for investigating the efficacy of an intervention [2]. Although RCTs are designed to identify a study population with stringent eligibility criteria (inclusion/exclusion criteria) to minimise bias and confounding and enhance internal validity of the findings, enrolling patients for RCTs often remains a challenge due to these criteria [2]. A second consequence of restrictive eligibility criteria is that trials do not capture a fully representative sample from the target population who may benefit from or be treated with the investigational drug or biologic of interest after approval, thereby raising concerns regarding the generalisability of results [2].

Using prospective real-world data from a geographically diverse, physician-diagnosed, severe asthma cohort treated by allergist-immunologists or pulmonologists in the USA, this study examined the modifying effects of nine baseline characteristics often used, or strongly considered for use (i.e. fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FENO)) in the RCTs as eligibility criteria on the association of biologic initiation and severe asthma exacerbations (represented in a causal directed acyclic graph in supplementary figure S1). The aim of this study was to quantify between-group comparisons of RCT-derived criteria on the association between biologic initiation and risk of severe asthma exacerbations. Thus, we wanted to identify which of these criteria could be relaxed to help recruitment and generalisability, without compromising the probability of trial success. Given the limitations of using real-world data (e.g. lack of proper control groups to compare to treatment groups, as well as confounding-related issues), the present study utilised a self-controlled case series design (SCCS), an analytical framework designed to assess effectiveness of within-individual pre- and post-biologic treatment while controlling for an individual's time-invariant confounders [14, 15]. We hypothesised that treatment effects would statistically vary across subgroups defined by RCT-derived criteria; if they do not, then the exclusion of patients based on them may be unwarranted. As future trials are likely to investigate medicines with novel mechanisms, we studied all existing FDA-approved asthma biologics in a pooled manner.

sec.title: Data sources, study design and patient selection
sec.p: This study used data from the CHRONICLE study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT03373045), a real-world, prospective, noninterventional, multicentre study of patients (aged ≥18 years) in the USA with confirmed severe asthma and treated by subspecialists (allergist-immunologists or pulmonologists) [16]. CHRONICLE first enrolled eligible patients with severe asthma for ≥12 months on 28 February 2018, from 132 sites. Patients were followed until death, loss to follow-up, withdrawal or completion, whichever came first. The present study utilised healthcare professional reported data based on medical record review of patients’ demographics, medical history, clinical measures, asthma history, smoking history, comorbidities, and current asthma management. For each patient, the participating sites provided the start and end dates of patients’ severe asthma exacerbations and asthma treatment history during the 12 months prior to enrolment, with prospective data collection from medical record extraction regularly following enrolment. The study protocol received central institutional review board (Advarra, Columbia, MD, USA) approval on 3 November 2017, and was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03373045) on 14 December 2017. Written informed consent for participation and acquisition of medical records was obtained at enrolment.

sec.title: Outcome variable
sec.p: The main outcome of interest was severe asthma exacerbations. We defined a severe asthma exacerbation as worsening of asthma symptoms that led to any of the following: 1) use of systemic corticosteroids for ≥3 days (with or without unscheduled/urgent care visits or emergency department visits lasting <24 h) or 2) an inpatient hospitalisation (defined as admission to an inpatient facility and/or evaluation and treatment in healthcare facility for ≥24 h) due to asthma.

sec.title: Exposure variable
sec.p: We defined the main exposure variable as exposure to any of the six FDA-approved biologics: omalizumab (NCT00314574), mepolizumab (NCT01691521), reslizumab (NCT01287039; NCT01285323), benralizumab (NCT01928771; NCT01914757), dupilumab (NCT02414854), and tezepelumab (NCT03347279). As such, for the purpose of this study patients who switched or combined biologics with a gap of ≤30 days would be counted as continually exposed to asthma biologic.

sec.title: Potential effects modifiers
sec.p: For our main analysis, we study effect modification of all eight characteristics commonly used as eligibility criteria in RCTs that were also recorded in CHRONICLE, with no further selection criteria. Additionally, while not an eligibility criterion for clinical trials we also considered FENO a common biomarker and predictor of biologic response that is being considered as an eligibility criterion for future studies. Although CHRONICLE measured these characteristics from 12 months prior to enrolment date, the present study used follow-up data to obtain measurements within the 12 months prior to first biologic initiation (index date). We used RCT-derived criteria to categorise the nine covariates into binary subgroups. These included 1) smoking pack-years (inclusion: <10 years versus exclusion: ≥10 years); 2) COPD presence (inclusion: no versus exclusion: yes); 3) bronchiectasis presence (inclusion: no versus exclusion: yes); 4) number of exacerbations in the past year (inclusion: two or more versus exclusion: fewer than two); 5) blood eosinophil count (BEC) (inclusion: ≥300 cells·µL−1 versus exclusion: <300 cells·µL−1); 6) FENO (inclusion: ≥50 ppb versus exclusion: <50 ppb); 7) forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) percentage predicted (inclusion: <80% pred versus exclusion: ≥80% pred); 8) FEV1 % reversibility (inclusion: ≥12% versus exclusion: <12%); and 9) FEV1/forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio (inclusion: <80% versus exclusion: ≥80%). Smoking pack-years was calculated as (number of cigarettes per day/20)×number of years smoked [17].

sec.title: Statistical analysis: self-controlled case-series
sec.p: This study included cases of patients who experienced any severe asthma exacerbations and received any biologic between February 2018 and October 2024. CHRONICLE collected data on exacerbation history and treatment history within 12 months prior to enrolment and regularly thereafter. To compare periods with and without biologic treatment, we included patients who experienced any severe asthma exacerbations and initiated any of the six biologics on or after CHRONICLE study initiation on 28 February 2018 (figure 1). The index date was used for defining the exposure variable. We excluded patients who initiated any of the biologics prior to the CHRONICLE enrolment date from the analysis. We defined the observation period as the period from observation start (a 12-month period prior to the index date) through the observation end (a 30-day period after the last biologic treatment administration). The 30-day extension period after the last biologic administration was added to capture any delayed effects [18]. The 12-month period prior to index date was classified as the baseline or unexposed period, whereas the period on biologic treatment from index date to observation end was defined as the exposed period (risk period).

caption.p: Analytical framework. This figure illustrates a single patient observation period.

sec.p: We generated summary statistics (proportions for the categorical variables and mean±sd for continuous variables) of patient sociodemographic and clinical measures at index date. The SCCS design is a case-only study design that estimates the relative rate of an outcome within a person rather than between people, with each person contributing to both the exposed and unexposed observation times [15, 19, 20]. We assumed that biologic treatment was continuous, and an individual's follow-up time was censored at early withdrawal, death or loss to follow-up. We aimed to minimise misclassification bias by censoring the follow-up time at early withdrawal, which was based on the assumption of independent (non-informative) censoring [14, 15]. As the SCCS design assesses the within-person comparisons (individuals serve as their own control), all time-fixed covariates (e.g. sex, ethnicity/race and genetic) whether measured or unmeasured are cancelled out in the design [15, 19, 20].

The SCCS design is formally derived from a Poisson process. Therefore, to investigate the effectiveness of biologics on the outcome, we fit conditional Poisson regression models to estimate incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% confidence intervals during the exposed period compared with unexposed period. We added an offset term (a natural logarithm of the interval) to account for the differences in period interval [15, 19, 20].

To validate results from the SCCS, we conducted a meta-analysis using recommended doses of six FDA-approved biologics from their pivotal RCTs retrieved from ClinicalTrials.gov database and compared the pooled estimate with our IRRs from the CHRONICLE cohort using SCCS. Thus, we systematically identified all six FDA-approved biologics by their unique clinical trial registration numbers on ClinicalTrials.gov. For each RCT (one or two per approved dose of biologic were found), we extracted rate ratios of the recommended-dose biologic compared with placebo. The pooled estimate was calculated using a random-effects model, and results were presented in a forest plot constructed with the “meta” package in R (default weighting within that package was used) [21]. Second, to infer the contribution of eligibility criteria, we investigated between-group comparisons (ratio of IRR) using RCT-derived cut-off points (inclusion versus exclusion) of the nine covariates separately in SCCS, with the exclusion criterion as a reference category. Thus, we included the interaction term between the exposure variable and binary covariate of interest (i.e. exposure×covariate) in the model [15]. A significant interaction term (p<0.05) suggests that the covariate of interest is an effect modifier, whereas statistically a nonsignificant interaction term (p≥0.05) suggests that covariate of interest may not be an effect modifier (at least at the given cut-off). To estimate the percentage of patients affected by RCT-derived criteria, we calculated the percentage of patients with the criteria for the statistically nonsignificant effect modifiers. The results were visualised using the “ComplexHeatmap” package in R [22].

To assess the robustness of our findings, we conducted several sensitivity analyses. First, we evaluated the effect of treatment duration on the outcome by varying the observation periods according to treatment exposure. In the primary analysis, we assessed outcomes over an individual's entire treatment duration. However, in the sensitivity analyses, we examined outcomes for treatment durations beyond 6 months, within 12 months, and beyond 12 months, each compared with a 12-month unexposed period. Second, we assessed different FEV1 (% predicted) cut-off points. Finally, we assessed within- and between-group comparisons based on seven sociodemographic characteristics, including sex, race, body mass index (BMI, kg·m−2), residence location, primary insurance, subspeciality care and exposure to allergens.

All statistical tests were two-tailed, and a p-value <0.05 was considered to represent statistical significance. Analyses were conducted in R (version 4.3.1). We used the “SCCS” package for data reshaping, event counts, and person-years calculation, and “gnm” package was used for estimating conditional Poisson regression model [15, 23].

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between 28 February 2018 and 28 October 2024, the CHRONICLE study enrolled 4503 patients with severe asthma across 132 participating sites. Of these, 3347 individuals received biologic treatment (prevalent or incident use). We excluded 2743 patients who had initiated biologic therapy prior to CHRONICLE enrolment and 124 who did not experience a severe asthma exacerbation leading to the outcome of interest. The final analytic cohort comprised 480 patients from 85 sites (figure 2).

caption.p: Flowchart for case ascertainment. #: emergency department visits, hospitalisation, unscheduled/urgent care visits or oral corticosteroid bursts for ≥3 days (time frame: 28 February 2017 to 28 February 2025).

sec.p: The mean±sd age at enrolment was 53.4±14.8 years, with a mean±sd age at biologic initiation of 54.7±14.9 years, and a mean±sd age at asthma diagnosis of 30.7±21.6 years. Of the cohort, 329 (68.5%) were female and 151 (31.5%) were male. Most patients were White (n=354, 73.8%), with 126 (26.3%) identifying as non-White. Among 479 individuals with recorded ethnicity, 442 (92.3%) were non-Hispanic and 37 (7.7%) were Hispanic or Latino. Bodyweight prior to biologic initiation was available for 458 patients, and 456 (99.6%) weighed >40 kg. BMI data were available for 434 patients, among whom 276 (63.6%) had a BMI of ≥30 kg·m−2, and 158 (36.4%) had a BMI <30 kg·m−2. Regarding smoking status, 308 (64.2%) were nonsmokers, 147 (30.6%) were former smokers, and 25 (5.2%) were current smokers at enrolment (table 1).

sec.p: Asthma biologic therapies were associated with a significant reduction in exacerbations across both RCT settings and real-world practice as assessed through the CHRONICLE data. The pooled rate ratio for exacerbation reduction from the meta-analysis of six RCTs using FDA-approved recommended doses was 0.53 (95% CI 0.47–0.60) (figure 3), indicating a 47% reduction in the risk of exacerbation compared with placebo. In our SCCS analysis leveraging CHRONICLE data, initiation of asthma biologics was associated with an IRR of 0.43 (95% CI 0.39–0.48) for exacerbations during the biologic-exposed period compared with the nonexposed period (table 2).

sec.p: In assessments of between-group comparisons (expressed as a ratio of ratios, 95% CI) in CHRONICLE used RCT criteria, with exclusion criteria as the reference, four criteria showed statistically significant differences, while five criteria showed statistically nonsignificant between-group comparisons (table 2 and figure 4). Specifically, statistically significant differences in asthma biologic effectiveness were seen with smoking pack-years (inclusion: <10 pack-years, 0.39 (0.35–0.44); exclusion: ≥10 pack-years, 0.78 (0.60–1.00); and between-group comparisons, 0.50 (0.38–0.66)); number of exacerbations in the past 12 months (inclusion: ≥2, 0.66 (0.50–0.86); exclusion: 1, 0.32 (0.28–0.36); and between-group comparisons, 0.49 (0.36–0.65)); FENO (inclusion: ≥50 ppb, 0.28 (0.20–0.39); exclusion: <50 ppb, 0.44 (0.37–0.54); and between-group comparisons, 0.63 (0.42–0.92)); and BEC (inclusion: ≥300 cells·µL−1, 0.32 (0.26–0.39); exclusion: <300 cells·µL−1, 0.49 (0.43–0.57); and between-group comparisons, 0.65 (0.51–0.82)). Conversely, the five criteria that showed statistically nonsignificant between-group comparisons were COPD presence (inclusion: no, 0.44 (0.39–0.49); exclusion: yes, 0.56 (0.45–0.71); and between-group comparison, 0.77 (0.59–1.01)); bronchiectasis presence (inclusion: no, 0.46 (0.41–0.51); exclusion: yes, 0.49 (0.31–0.77); and between-group comparisons, 0.94 (0.59–1.49)); FEV1% predicted (inclusion: <80%, 0.42 (0.36–0.48); exclusion: ≥80%, 0.38 (0.31–0.46); and between-group comparisons, 1.11 (0.87–1.43)); FEV1% reversibility (inclusion: ≥12%, 0.54 (0.42–0.68); exclusion: <12%, 0.50 (0.40–0.63); and between-group comparisons, 1.06 (0.77–1.48)); and FEV1/FVC ratio (inclusion: <80%, 0.40 (0.35–0.46); exclusion: ≥80%, 0.43 (0.35–0.53); and between-group comparisons, 0.93 (0.72–1.20)) (figure 4 and table 2).

sec.p: Of the five criteria showing nonsignificant between-group comparisons, FEV1 % reversibility excluded the most patients (66.7%), followed by FEV1 % predicted (35.9%), and FEV1/FVC (28.1%), COPD (15.0%) and bronchiectasis (5.2%) (figure 5).

caption.p: Heatmap illustrating the ratio of incidence rate ratios (IRR) and percentage of patients affected by randomised controlled trial cut-off thresholds. FEV1: forced expiratory volume in 1 s; FVC: forced vital capacity.

sec.p: Our results were robust in sensitivity analyses, in that 1) incident biologic users who did not exacerbate had similar characteristics to those who did (table 1); 2) treatment duration did not meaningfully alter the estimate of treatment effectiveness (supplementary table S1); 3) no statistically significant treatment effect modification was seen at either FEV1 % predicted cut-offs of 75%, 80%, 85% or 90% (table 2 and supplementary table S2); and 4) no sociodemographic factors studied other than residence location and exposure to allergens were found to modify treatment effectiveness (supplementary table S3).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Both RCTs and the CHRONICLE study have previously demonstrated that treatment with biologics substantially reduce asthma exacerbation risk [24–27]. Our meta-analysis of RCTs and our analysis of CHRONICLE confirm this finding. A 57% reduction in exacerbation rates with biologic treatment compared with the period before biologic initiation is consistent with the pooled RCT meta-analysis estimate, which showed a significant 47% exacerbation rate reduction in patients receiving biologics compared with those receiving placebo. This general agreement between RCT and real-world evidence is encouraging and increases our confidence in subsequent findings [26]. The slightly higher effect size with real-world evidence SCCS than RCTs is probably attributable to differences in the treated populations and regression-to-the-mean bias, as patients are more likely to have an exacerbation in the pre-biologic period when having one increases the chance of receiving biologic treatment.

In the eligibility criteria assessment using SCCS and RCT-derived threshold values, we identified several important clinical and biomarker-based modifiers of biologic effectiveness. Greater treatment benefit was observed among those with more frequent recent exacerbations (ratio of IRR 0.49), minimal smoking pack-years (ratio of IRR 0.50), and higher levels of type 2 inflammatory biomarkers (FENO and BEC). This evidence aligns with established understanding that chronic tobacco exposure and reduced type 2 inflammatory airway biology limit responsiveness to biologic therapy [27–29]. These results reinforce guideline recommendations for biomarker-guided patient selection and highlight the need for further work to optimise biologic use in tobacco-exposed individuals. Conversely, major indices of lung function (FEV1 % predicted, FEV1 % reversibility and FEV1/FVC ratio) did not significantly modify biologic effectiveness. This was also seen with comorbid COPD or bronchiectasis, but we cannot rule out weak effect modification and regulators will likely continue to require exclusion for these alternative conditions. Although prior studies have variably reported the impact of airflow obstruction and comorbid respiratory disease on biologic efficacy, our findings derived from a real-world dataset reflective of routine clinical practice suggest that these factors do not strongly modify biologic effects on exacerbation risk [30].

Strict spirometry-based exclusion criteria are often chosen in trials of asthma biologics to select a population in which the impact of biologics on lung function (often a secondary end-point) can be detected. Our findings show that strict spirometry-based exclusion criteria preclude a large proportion of real-world patients from participating in clinical trials without evidence for differential benefit [2]. This highlights a trade-off between the desire to show the impact of biologics on lung function and to avoid exclusion of patients from trials. As lung function improvement could be evaluated in a robust, pre-specified manner in the subset of those with reduced lung function at baseline, the use of RCT exclusions based on spirometry should be reconsidered.

The observed effect modification by exacerbation history underscores the value of prior exacerbations as a stratification tool and as a marker of uncontrolled disease activity, whereas significant differences across FENO and BEC strata support growing evidence for the predictive utility of these biomarkers in biologic therapy selection [29]. It is worth noting that as FENO and BEC status are associated with exacerbation risk, estimates of their effect modification in our SCCS analysis may be confounded by time-varying factors (such as acute worsening of asthma) that simultaneously influence biomarker levels, treatment decisions, and propensity for exacerbation. Clinically, this means patients with elevated FENO or BEC may be tested and thus classified during periods of heightened disease activity, making it challenging to disentangle whether observed differences in treatment response reflect true effect modification or the influence of transient changes in underlying risk.

By excluding a significant proportion of patients who may receive benefit from and are eligible to receive asthma biologics post-approval, several RCT eligibility criteria, particularly those based on spirometry, appear to be overly restrictive. Using the RCT threshold cut-off levels, we observed that 66.7%, 35.9% and 28.1% of patients who may have benefited from the trial were excluded due to their FEV1 % reversibility, FEV1 % predicted and FEV1/FVC ratio, respectively. Our findings, which require validation in a larger, more representative and better controlled study, highlight that relaxing exclusion criteria on lung function tests could benefit trial recruitment without compromising trial success, assuming these changes would be acceptable to regulators.

While not the focus of this study, it was interesting to observe an association between treatment effectiveness and both allergen exposure and residence location. The latter may relate to the fact that asthma tends to be different in rural communities and possibly less severe.

The present study has several key limitations. First, as a real-world evidence study without randomisation, there is risk of residual confounding by time-varying confounders. The consistency we see between estimates of the effect of biologics between RCTs and CHRONICLE suggests that any such confounding is within acceptable limits. Second, our study had a relatively small sample size, which limited our power to detect weak effect modification. Using CHRONICLE allowed us to study variables such as FENO, which is not typically recorded within datasets with a larger sample size, such as health record or insurance datasets. However, its design meant that many participants were already on biologics at enrolment; these patients were excluded from our analysis, raising the risk of selection bias and increasing the need for validation. Third, our focus on pooled biologic treatment meant we did not account for the different indicated groups of each biologic, nor did we relate treatment effect modification to mechanism. However, this allowed us to identify eligibility criteria that appeared to be overly restrictive across multiple mechanisms to better inform the design of trials for treatments of mechanisms that may be novel. Fourth, we did not assess body weight as an eligibility criterion because 99.6% of patients with bodyweight >40 kg fell into one category, which made it unsuitable for between-group comparisons. For this reason, we used BMI in the sensitivity analysis and the result was consistent. Future analyses in larger cohorts, such as the International Severe Asthma Registry, could help with most of the limitations listed, by decreasing selection bias while increasing statistical power overall which could allow the detection of biologic specific treatment modification.

The strength of our investigation is that, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to assess the impact of RCT-derived criteria in severe asthma with a range of characteristics, including lifestyle, clinical spirometry measures, and biomarkers in real-world settings using a within-person analytical framework while adjusting for time-fixed covariates [15]. In addition, a series of sensitivity analyses with varied FEV1 % predicted cut-off points, treatment durations, and sociodemographic features yielded similar results to the main findings, which again supports the agreement between the RCTs and the SCCS from the CHRONICLE study.

In conclusion, this study affirms the effectiveness of asthma biologics in clinical practice; highlights the importance of exacerbation history, smoking pack-years and type 2 biomarker levels for patient selection; and questions the role of spirometry-focused exclusion criteria. Relaxing respiratory comorbidity (COPD and bronchiectasis) and spirometry-based (FEV1 % predicted, FEV1 % reversibility, and FEV1/FVC ratio) criteria could help capture a broader population of patients found in real-world clinical practice who may benefit from biologic therapies or other advanced interventions.
